swanhanger.claim: Saniger is a worn-down form of SWANHANGER, and the older spelling is on record for five hundred years.
swanhanger.proof: One deed, catalogued twice. Berkeley Castle holds it as BCM/A/1/24/185, 11 April 51 Edw. III (1377), 'Elias de Swonhongre and William Panyter'. Birmingham Archives holds a copy as MS 3549/20, same day, same parties, and calls the land 'a messuage, land and appurtenances in SWANHANGER, co. Glouc.'
swanhanger.gloss: Gloucestershire Archives settles it outright in D654/III/9: 'Messuage called Oldminsters in SWANHANGER ... [Saniger in Hinton]'. The archivist supplied the modern name in brackets.
forms: C 131/202/27 — 'William Swannanger of Swannanger in Glos., esquire'

Sanigar Farm, Sharpness; Sanigar Lane, Hinton
swanhanger.people: Three forenames carry the older spelling: Thomas de Swonhungre (24 entries), John (10) and William (8) — a family that had already taken its name from the place by about 1300, five centuries before anyone in this archive was born.
swanhanger.field: Thomas de Swonhungre granted land in WESTFELD in the early 14th century (BCM/A/1/65/18). John Saniger released three acres in WESTFIELD, Saniger, in 1601. Edward Saniger exchanged three-quarters of an acre in WESTFIELD in 1716. One field, four hundred years, three spellings of one name.

estate.reading: In 1692 Edward Saniger is a CLOTHIER. In 1709 the same man at the same address is a GENT. Bigland, writing later, calls him 'Edward Saniger of Saniger, Gent.' and records his wife Esther's death in June 1693. The deeds show the promotion; the gravestone shows the household it happened to.

neighbours.note: Bigland's Berkeley monuments name six more households as 'of Saniger'. None of them is called Saniger. A hamlet, not a family seat.

hinton: Bigland describes the tithing in 1791: “4. Hinton, wherein are Wanswell, a reputed Manor … SANIGER, long held by an old Family of the same Name, in which also is another Estate belonging to WOODWARD: Hinton, Halmore; and Breadstone.” The Woodward estate is not a guess — Daniel Woodward of Bristol, wine merchant, leased Panthurst in Saniger in 1749, and the deed is D2957/41/58.

smyth.head: The steward of Berkeley says it himself, in 1639
smyth.lede: This archive argued from deeds that Saniger is a worn-down Swanhanger. It did not need to argue. John Smyth of Nibley, steward of the Berkeley estates, wrote the survey of the hundred in about 1639, and gave the hamlet its own heading.
smyth.quoteSrc: A Description of the Hundred of Berkeley, folio 365 — printed 1885 as volume 3 of The Berkeley Manuscripts
smyth.means: The hamlet is no longer just a place name with deeds attached. It has thirteen houses, a resident family in five named generations, a freeholder in 1541 dealing with a baron's manor, and a trustee holding land for other men.

hamlet.head: Thirteen houses
hamlet.body: Smyth describes the place exactly: “a small hamblet parcell of that Manor of Hame, lyinge within the ffalloe therof, confiftinge of 13. dwellinge houfes; The moft eminent wherof is the inheritance of John Swonhunger ats Sanyger.”
hamlet.means: Thirteen houses, inside the manor of Hame, inside the parish of Berkeley. The manor's other hamlets are listed alongside it — “Wike ats Wikes-elme, Wanefwell, Swonhunger ats Saniger, Halmer ats Ecton, and Egeton: All of them within the parifh of Berkeley”. Halmer is HALMORE, where the 1608 muster puts John Saniger, labourer.
hamlet.split: The hamlet straddled two manors, which is why the 1608 survey files it under Hinton: Smyth lists the manor of Hinton as holding “part of Swonhunger, ats Saniger”, along with Oldminster, Kingshill and Ridlesford.

pedigree.head: Five generations, named
pedigree.body: Smyth then does the thing this archive has wanted from every source it has opened. He names the owner and walks back up the male line:
pedigree.quote: And the faid John Swonhunger ats Saniger that nowe is, a° 1639, is fonne of John who died, fonne of Maurice who died, fonne of Robert who died, fonne of William who died.
rows: “the moft eminent” house in the hamlet; held of the manor of Hame by knight service, suit of court, and rent of 6s to Hame and 12d to Hinton
died; no date given — the lands were bought from Thomas Lewes als Davis by deeds of 10, 12 and 14 Henry VIII, which is 1518–1523
pedigree.means: Four generations above a man living in 1639, in a named place, with the tenure and the rents. Smyth gives no dates for the four, but he dates the purchase of the land to 1518–1523, which puts William in the reign of Henry VIII.
pedigree.careful: This is a freeholding family, and that matters when reading it against the muster. In 1608 the hamlet also held JOHN SAINGER, weaver — a man of the same name in the same thirteen houses, and not necessarily of the same house.

senior.head: And the older line, which ended in a daughter
senior.body: The Swonhungers of 1639 were, in Smyth's words, “a yonger branch difcended from the ancient old owners”. The senior line is traceable much further and ended much earlier: Elias Swonhunger, then Elias his son who died in 13 Richard II, then John Swonhungre, who “died without iffue in 3. H. 4.” — 1401 or 1402 — leaving his sisters Isable and Elizabeth his heirs. Isable married John Thorpe, and the main estate went into the name of Thorpe for two hundred years.
senior.earlier: Earlier still the name is a witness name in the Berkeley deeds: Thomas de Swonhungre attests charters of Thomas Lord Berkeley under the third Edward, and William Swonhungre appears in 1353 as “cofyn et vn des heires” of Thomas de Stone.

two.head: Two more men of the name, with dates
rows: Party to a quadripartite indenture of 33 Henry VIII with Richard Hickes and Thomas Griffith, buying a manor from William Lord Stourton — “then inrolled in the Chancery”. He later sold his part to William Laverance als Lawrance.

Named as one of three trustees — with Mathewe Smyth of Wanswell and Robert Atkins of Newport — in the sale of “almoft all the faid ffarmes and lands”, granting them on to particular lessees “according to the truft repofed in them”.

smyth.careful: And it still does not reach Hannah. Nothing here connects the Swonhungers of the hamlet to the weavers and labourers of Cam and Dursley, or to the woman baptised at Berkeley in 1804. The gap is unbridged, and this does not bridge it — it only makes clear what the name was attached to before it was a surname in a register.
smyth.where: Read 14 September 2026 in the full text of the 1885 edition on the Internet Archive (berkeleymanuscri03smyt), which is out of copyright and downloads freely. Smyth's index carries about twenty-five further page references under “Swanhunger” that have not yet been read.

catalogue.head: Seventy-one records, and the ones nobody here had seen
catalogue.lede: The National Archives' Discovery catalogue indexes what other repositories hold as well as its own. Searched on 14 September 2026 for every spelling, it returns seventy-one records under Saniger alone — and a run of Berkeley Castle deeds naming people “of Saniger” from before 1291 to 1473.
new: Maurice Saniger and Jane his wife

D2957/41/181 — a fine: “John Hardinge, quer. Maurice Saniger and Jane his wife, Maria Stiffe, and William Perratt”. A named couple in the hamlet, a century after Smyth's pedigree ended, and a Maurice — the same forename Smyth gives as the 1639 owner's grandfather.

GDR/B4/1/387 — a defamation suit in the Gloucester consistory court. Church-court defamation cases are almost always brought by women over sexual slander, and the files usually carry depositions naming neighbours, ages and abodes.
The 1617 trustee deed, dated at last

D2957/41/64 — a conveyance naming Mathew Smith of Wanswell, Robert Atkins of Newport and John Saniger. Smyth describes exactly this transaction in the Hundred of Berkeley but gives it no date; the catalogue supplies one.
D2957/41/18 — a release to John Smithe of Panthurste. The earliest dated document this archive holds in which a man carries the name as a surname, and it calls him a yeoman.
CO1/I/2/B/6 — a coroner's inquest for the Lower Division. Cam is the second commonest Saniger parish in this archive's register work, with twenty entries.
Inquisition post mortem of Henry Mallett
MS 3549/187 at Birmingham — a minor, proving what he held at his death. It surfaces under Swanhanger, and the Malletts appear repeatedly beside the Sanigers in the Berkeley deeds.

trap.head: And one thing not to read off this list
trap.body: It looks as though the spelling SANIGER is attested from before 1291, which would overturn what this archive says about the forms. It is not. The place name in these entries is the modern cataloguer's standard form, supplied for searchability; the personal names are given as the documents write them, which is why Swonhungre, Swonhongre and Swannanger all survive in the same list. A catalogue description is evidence of what a record is about, not of how it is spelled.
trap.chip: a catalogue is not a transcript

catalogue.means: The hamlet has been a place people were named after for at least seven hundred and thirty-five years, and the Berkeley muniments name a dozen of them.
catalogue.careful: None of this reaches Hannah either, and the gap it does not close is the same one: these are Berkeley freeholders, tenants and litigants, and the woman baptised there in 1804 descends from weavers and labourers whose link to them is unproved.
catalogue.next: Unread and worth reading: the three Berkeley Castle groupings the catalogue names but does not itemise — “The Saniger purparty in Ham”, “The Saniger purparty in Wanswell” and “Acquisition of the Skinner holding in Saniger” — and GDR/B4/1/387, the 1768 defamation file.
